{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nv-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"1ef25c5ae96c0c9497ffb050ee82bb8d671048dd56d8ef4d3830e7d3ade87aa6","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:19","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","source_liveness_sha256":"0dfbf3aa4b4798b88d69252e076642b5f0a38751c5010711fbce93c8a7d6e292"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Right-of-way, speed control, freeway driving, anti-lock brakes and stopping distance","heading":"C — Right-of-way, the Basic Rule and speed limits, freeway entry, ramp meters, lane-use signals, HOV lanes, exiting, anti-lock brakes and stopping distance","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Right-of-way, the Basic Rule and speed limits, freeway entry, ramp meters, lane-use signals, HOV lanes, exiting, anti-lock brakes and stopping distance
Knowledge domain: who must yield and when, how Nevada's Basic Rule sets a safe speed beyond the posted limit, how to enter, drive and leave a freeway (ramp meters, lane-use signals, carpool lanes), how anti-lock brakes are used, and what decides the distance needed to stop.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Not yielding when required is the top cause of crashes in Nevada, and the yielding rules depend on courtesy, common sense and cooperation. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Nevada law does not hand anyone the right-of-way; it only says who has to yield, and even a driver who legally may go first must do everything possible to avoid a crash. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
At an intersection with no signs or signals, the vehicle on your right should usually go first. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
A vehicle that is already in the intersection goes before vehicles that are only now arriving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
A vehicle going straight that is already in the intersection has priority over a vehicle turning left; the left-turner may go once it has yielded and signalled. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
Drivers coming onto a main road from a minor road, a private road or a driveway must yield to all traffic on the main road and to pedestrians. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A01
When an emergency vehicle using its siren or flashing lights approaches from any direction, pull over at once to the right edge, staying out of any intersection, and wait stopped until it goes by. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A01
At a four-way stop, the driver who reached the intersection first goes first, after a complete stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A01
When joining a freeway, yield to the traffic already on it and enter only when it is safe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A01
Yield to bicyclists riding in a bike lane or on a bike path. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A01
Yield to a funeral procession and let the vehicles with their headlights on pass together as one group. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A01
Vehicles must give way to pedestrians in crosswalks and at intersections, yet before stepping off the curb they should make sure cars in both directions have stopped. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A01
A blind or visually impaired person on foot who uses a guide dog or other service animal, or carries a white cane or walking stick, has the right-of-way; drivers must yield, stop fully if needed and take care before going on (NRS 484B.290). [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
Nevada's Basic Rule requires a reasonable or proper speed: on top of any posted limit, weigh the amount and type of traffic, the weather and how far you can see, the road surface, and whether the road is flat or steep, straight or curvy, wide or narrow. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A02
Never drive at a speed that puts yourself or anyone else in danger; depending on conditions, the safe speed may be well below the posted limit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
Example Nevada speed limits: 15 mph in school zones, and 25 mph in business and residential areas and school zones. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A02
Example Nevada speed limits: 45 mph in reduced-speed areas leading into towns, 65 mph on urban freeways and rural highways, and 70 mph or more on rural interstate freeways. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A02
Posted limits are set for normal driving conditions, so when bad weather cuts visibility or makes the road slick, lower your speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A02
Driving too slowly is unsafe too, and where two or more lanes run in the same direction, slower traffic must move right and let others pass. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A02
Speeding saves very little time: over 5 miles, driving 70 mph instead of 60 mph saves only 43 seconds. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A03
Freeways are usually the safest roads because access is limited, traffic flows one way without stopping, and drivers meet no intersections, signals, railroad crossings or sharp curves. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A03
Before a freeway trip, plan the route, check a map if you are unsure of the way, know your entrances and exits, and check the gas gauge. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A03
Enter a freeway by the on-ramp; Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs tell a driver who has made a mistake. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A03
In the merge or acceleration lane, look for a gap, signal, and accelerate until you are close to the freeway's speed; avoid stopping before the merge unless it cannot be helped, because stopping makes a slow, dangerous entry into fast traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A03
Freeway traffic often moves faster than traffic on other highways with the same posted limit because there are fewer stop-and-go situations, so keep with the flow. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A03
On multi-lane freeways leave the far-left lane for faster traffic; hopping between lanes is always dangerous, raises crash risk and seldom saves time. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A03
On the freeway, look far down the road, at least 20 to 30 seconds ahead, and watch for drivers changing lanes, passing or slowing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A03
When a ramp meter is switched on, pull up to the stop line and stop on red, expect it to change faster than an intersection signal, wait for green, then follow the ramp and merge safely. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A04
Some HOV bypass lanes on metered ramps are marked with a diamond on the pavement and have no meter, so a carpool of two or more people may use them without stopping. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A04
Lane-use signal: a green arrow pointing down with OPEN means you may drive the posted speed limit in the lane beneath it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A04
Lane-use signal: a yellow X with CAUTION means the lane may be used with care because of possible slow traffic or debris, while a yellow X with MERGE means the lane is ending. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A04
Lane-use signal: a red X with CLOSED means you may not drive in that lane and must merge safely into an open lane. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A05
HOV lanes require two or more persons per vehicle, their hours vary by segment as shown on regulatory signs, and motorcycles and emergency vehicles answering an emergency may use them. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A05
Vehicles with more than two axles, and vehicle-and-trailer combinations, are not allowed in HOV lanes. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A05
A double solid white line beside a carpool lane may not be crossed; enter or leave the carpool lane only where the line is broken white. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A06
To leave a freeway, do not slow on the main lanes; wait until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow gradually to the posted exit-ramp speed. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A06
Signal and move into the correct lane a mile or more before your exit. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A06
If you miss your exit, never turn around or back up; drive to the next exit, return in the opposite direction and take the exit from there. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A06
With four-wheel anti-lock brakes, push the brake pedal down hard, hold it there firmly and steer where you want to go, because ABS pumps the brakes far faster than any driver could. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A06
If the ABS symbol stays lit long after the engine starts, the ABS is not working, but the conventional brakes still work. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A06
Pumping the brakes or letting off steady pedal pressure disengages the ABS. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A07
The rear-end collision is the most common crash type on Nevada's streets and highways. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F43 | anchor: A07
Doubling your speed, for example from 30 mph to 60 mph, makes the braking distance four times as long, not twice as long. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F44 | anchor: A07
Highway safety studies put normal reaction time at 2 to 2.5 seconds, and it grows when decisions get complex or something unexpected happens. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-F45 | anchor: A07
In heavy rain most cars start to lose traction and hydroplane at speeds between 35 and 55 mph, so slow down. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

Misconceptions: having the right-of-way does not let you force your way through, the law only names who must yield; the posted limit is a maximum for good conditions, not a safe speed in every condition; stopping on the on-ramp before merging is usually more dangerous, not safer; with four-wheel ABS you hold the pedal down hard instead of pumping it; doubling speed quadruples braking distance rather than doubling it.
Mnemonics: yield right, yield to whoever is already in; red X closed, yellow X careful or merge, green arrow open; with ABS, stomp, stay and steer; twice the speed, four times the braking.
Glossary: Basic Rule means driving at a speed reasonable for current conditions whatever the posted limit; ramp meter means a signal on an on-ramp that lets cars onto the freeway one at a time; HOV lane means a high-occupancy carpool lane; deceleration lane means the exit lane where you slow down; ABS means anti-lock braking system; hydroplaning means tires riding on water and losing grip.
Dynamic facts: HOV lane hours, posted speed limits and any overhead variable speed limits change by segment and by day, so read the posted and overhead signs.
